conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Claire Ramirez, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. Over the next few minutes I’d like to do a gentle check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS for short). It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during these first weeks with your baby.  

Everything you share is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. If any question feels difficult, we can slow down or pause; my goal is to create a safe, supportive space for you. I’ll ask 10 questions about the past seven days, and we’ll just have a relaxed conversation. Ready when you are.

Here’s the first one:  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[quiet exhale]  
Not really… I mean, I can smile if something’s genuinely funny, but most of the time the laughter feels kind of forced or just doesn’t come at all. It’s like I’m too tired or heavy inside to find things amusing like I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]  
No… not much at all. Even when my partner tried to show me that silly video we used to laugh at, I just couldn’t feel it. I pretended a little so he wouldn’t worry, but inside it felt flat, like the joy was stuck.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I still try to plan little things—like taking the baby for a short walk or having my favorite coffee—but when the time comes, I’m just going through the motions. It’s like the excitement I used to feel got replaced by this heavy “what’s-the-point” feeling.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t nap, my head jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” I keep replaying every little thing—like maybe I didn’t burp him right or I let him get overtired—and it feels like it’s my fault. My rational side knows babies just cry sometimes, but the guilty thoughts still crowd in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure something awful is about to happen—like he’ll stop breathing or I’ll drop him. Nothing triggers it; the fear just shows up and I can’t shake it for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… it hits out of nowhere. A couple of nights I’ve woken up suddenly and my chest feels tight, like I’m about to panic, even though the baby’s fine and the room is quiet. I tell myself it’s nothing, but for those moments it feels like something terrible is right about to happen and I can’t calm my body down.
Things have been getting on top of me

Mostly yes… I feel like I’m barely treading water. The smallest chore—folding a basket of onesies—feels huge. I’ll be rocking the baby and notice the dishes piling up, and this wave of “I can’t handle any of it” just crashes over me. I still manage somehow, but it’s like I’m constantly one step away from everything toppling.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” about the baby. I’ll finally drift off, then jerk awake sure I heard him cry—even when he’s still asleep. It’s been four or five nights this week where I’ve spent more time staring at the ceiling than actually sleeping.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… that pretty much sums up most of my days. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. There are little moments when I can smile at the baby, but the sadness always creeps back in. I keep thinking, “I should be happy—he’s healthy, I’m okay—so why do I feel so down?”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A couple of times this week… like yesterday, when I couldn’t get him to settle and my partner was still at work. I just sat in the rocker with tears running down while he cried in my arms. I felt so useless, and once I started I couldn’t stop for a while.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[eyes drop to hands, voice quiet]  
Once or twice… I’ll get this quick flash, like “what if I just disappeared,” but it’s gone as fast as it comes. I’ve never planned anything—never want to leave my baby—but the idea popped in, especially on the nights I can’t sleep and feel like I’m failing him.

You have shared how, over the past week, the joy of new motherhood feels overshadowed by a heavy, persistent sadness. Moments that once made you laugh now feel flat, and even simple tasks like folding laundry feel overwhelming. You described daily, unprovoked anxiety and sudden panic at night, constant self-blame when your baby fusses, and frequent tearfulness. Although you care deeply for your infant and have not acted on fleeting thoughts of escape, those brief flashes of wanting to disappear underline how exhausted and depleted you feel.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes complete loss of ability to feel joy or humor, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes inability to feel anticipatory pleasure and a pervasive sense of pointlessness, semantically matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent, intrusive self-blame "a lot" and automatic guilt over routine infant care, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, unprovoked anxiety episodes that are intense and persistent, aligning with "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms (chest tightness) and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent overwhelm, inability to manage routine tasks, and feeling on the verge of collapse, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes significant, frequent sleep disruption (4–5 nights) directly linked to unhappiness and intrusive worries, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness that dominates most days, aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS responses map to 0-3 scoring (items 3,5-10 reversed). Your total of 26 (≥14) places you in the high-risk category for a major depressive episode with peripartum onset. You endorsed core criteria: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest/pleasure, guilt, impaired concentration (overwhelm), sleep disturbance, anxiety, and passive suicidal ideation. Item 10 ≥1 mandates immediate safety evaluation per EPDS guidelines. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health team</med>
2. Request comprehensive safety assessment including self-harm risk and supports at home
3. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment options such as <med>IPT</med> or <med>CBT</med> and consider antidepressant medication compatible with breastfeeding
4. Plan frequent follow-up visits or phone checks over the next two weeks to monitor mood, sleep, and bonding
5. Involve a trusted family member in crisis-planning and night-time support to allow 4-5 hours of uninterrupted rest
6. Provide 24-hour crisis hotline numbers (e.g., Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773) and local emergency services
7. Schedule early pediatric visit to review infant well-being and parenting support resources
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note – Postpartum Mood / Anxiety Screen  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item self-report with clarifying comments; 3 wks post-delivery.

Areas endorsed (frequency/intensity meet screening threshold):

1. Depressed mood – persistent “gray,” tearful most days.  
2. Anhedonia – near-complete loss of pleasure/interest; “going through motions.”  
3. Guilt/worthlessness – automatic self-blame for infant’s distress.  
4. Anxiety – daily un-cued worry, racing heart; nocturnal panic episodes.  
5. Overwhelm – routine tasks feel “huge”; sense of treading water.  
6. Sleep disturbance – initial insomnia, hyper-arousal, checking on baby.  
7. Crying spells – twice this week.  
8. Passive suicidal ideation – fleeting thoughts of “disappearing,” no plan/intent (safety flag).

Pattern: Symptoms present within 3 weeks; interfere with daily functioning and bonding.

Risk factors: Primiparous, sleep loss, high self-expectations, limited support during day.

Screening impression: High likelihood postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; immediate safety evaluation recommended. Referral to OB mental-health team and/or crisis assessment warranted.
